properties.decision:
CANDIDATE PATTERN, NOT A ROOT CAUSE — recorded as an idea because it has not been through the refutation step the root-cause skill requires, and the first plausible explanation is exactly what that skill exists to slow down.

Four of the findings from the 2026-08-31 field reports have the same shape. In each, reflow2 STATES the correct move in prose and offers a TYPED TOOL only for a different move — so the agent takes an untyped fallback, and the fallback leaves nothing any detector can read.

① `answer_gap` (musicjug). The gap text says "Write the answer into the design ... or acknowledge_gap." Only the second half has a tool. Fallback: acknowledge under the owner's name, or leave a solved gap open as noise.
② `depends_on` (musicjug). The loop asks for component dependencies; nine typed helpers exist and that one does not, while its obvious name is taken by cross-design version pinning. Fallback: raw `create_edge`.
③ Edge prose (bhome). Every `add_*` warns loudly on node overwrite and `reconcile_artifacts` catches file drift; nothing governs edge `evidence` or `note`. Fallback: repair by hand, if you happen to remember what the edge said.
④ Snapshot-before-revise (musicjug). The warning names the right order and holds the only copy of the replaced value. Fallback: an undo recipe, in a harness that emits parallel batches and cannot reliably honour call order anyway.

THE COMMON SHAPE, stated so it can be refuted: **the instruction layer is ahead of the typed-tool layer, and where it is ahead, the agent's fallback is invisible.** reflow2's own recorded doctrine says vocabulary reaches a design only with three legs — a typed tool, an instruction, and a detector that notices absence. In all four, leg two is present, leg one is missing, and leg three therefore cannot fire.
properties.name: OPEN — four findings in one day share a shape: reflow2's prose names the right move and only the OTHER move has a tool. Is that one defect or four?
properties.rationale:
WHY THIS MIGHT BE ONE THING AND NOT FOUR: the four repairs are independent and each is cheap on its own, so treating them separately loses nothing immediate. What it would lose is the fifth instance. If the pattern is real, the generative question is "where else does a reflow2 message tell somebody to do something no tool does?" — which is answerable by reading the instruction corpus against the tool surface, and would find the next four before a user does.

WHY IT MIGHT NOT BE ONE THING, and this is the honest counter: ② is a naming accident, ③ is a whole unbuilt governance layer for edges, ④ is a sequencing choice, and ① is a deliberate anti-forgery guard whose scope was drawn slightly too wide. Those have four different causes and share only a symptom — an agent doing the untyped thing. Grouping them could manufacture a "systemic defect" out of four ordinary gaps, which is precisely the over-engineering failure mode this project watches for. The count is four out of roughly a dozen findings; nobody has checked the other eight against the pattern, or checked how many typed tools DO have their instruction.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: read the served skill and tool prose for imperatives ("write the answer", "record the dependency", "snapshot first") and check each against the tool surface. If the hit rate is high, it is one thing. If these four are the whole set, they are four.

⚠️ THE CHEAPEST HALF IS INDEPENDENT OF THE ANSWER. All four individual repairs stand on their own merits and none of them waits on this question.
